A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TempoControl. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and rendered figures, are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original temporal-control experiments, loss ablations, qualitative generation results and a 50-participant preference study.

after.justification: v2 reports original temporal-control results, expanded baseline comparisons, component and weight ablations, qualitative examples and the retained preference-study results.

M1.justification: v1's four-component objective includes a separate spatial-consistency penalty anchoring attention to its pre-optimization state. v2 removes this penalty and its lambda3 weight from Section 4, Figure 3 and Algorithm 1, changing the optimization objective to three components. Renaming energy to magnitude does not otherwise change that component's formula.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the 80-class single-object evaluation, 82-pair two-object evaluation, 100-video motion evaluation, VBench multiple-object benchmark and simple audio-alignment scenarios. v2's complete category and prompt lists document existing coverage; the additional examples do not establish a distinct task or domain.

E2.justification: v1 Table 1 compares only against text-conditioned Wan 2.1 1.3B. v2 adds CogX1.5 5B, Wan2.1-L 14B and Wan2.2-TI2V 5B across all three temporal-control tasks; TempoControl still uses Wan 2.1 1.3B. Wan2.2 also joins the appendix prompt-phrasing comparison. MinT is discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: Table 1 narrows reporting from nine metrics to four, dropping subject consistency, background consistency, motion smoothness, dynamic degree and aesthetic quality for the temporal-control tasks; these results are not relocated to the appendix. Appendix .2 changes the object-task magnitude weight from 1 to 0.3. New single-object ablations introduce component combinations and weight sweeps, while the documented detector and frame-sampling procedures remain stable.

E4.justification: v1's two-object leave-one-component-out study and associated object-replacement examples are removed. v2 adds single-object correlation-only, entropy-only and combined-component comparisons in Table 3, magnitude/entropy weight sweeps in Appendix Table 6, and semantic-distortion examples in Figures 4 and 9. The prompt-phrasing analysis is also extended to Wan2.2.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests for its experiments. The preference-study sample size and aggregate reporting practice remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces TempoControl temporal accuracies of 81.00%, 55.00% and 53% with 82.50%, 52.93% and 57% for single-object, two-object and movement tasks. These accompany revised objectives/settings, so they are not controlled same-setting improvements. New baseline and ablation results are added. Prompt-phrasing results reverse the earlier accuracy trend: v1 slightly favors omitting timing cues, whereas v2 reports 82.50% with cues versus 78.75% without. Human-study and full VBench multiple-object scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The spatial-penalty definition in v1 Equation 9 is removed, and its four-term objective becomes v2's three-term Equation 9. This is a localized substantive change to the mathematical formulation. The remaining attention, correlation, magnitude, entropy and audio-processing definitions are retained; neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: v2's introduction explicitly claims the first inference-time method for temporally controlling specific words and emphasizes entropy regularization's preservation of semantic consistency. The central claims of training-free attention steering, temporal control with preserved video quality, and applicability to objects, motion and audio alignment remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantial qualifications about detector failures inflating absence accuracy, possible imaging-quality bias toward multi-object scenes, and semantic distortion under correlation-only optimization. It interprets entropy as potentially useful beyond temporal control and attributes improved use of timing phrases to its optimization. Appendix .4 newly reports annotator difficulty judging 1–2-second timing differences and acknowledges that the study was not repeated. Discussion of reduced dynamics disappears for the temporal-control tasks but remains for the constant-mask benchmark.

D1.justification: Appendix .3 newly specifies all 80 object classes, 82 object pairs and 100 action triplets, materially improving reconstruction of the evaluation inputs. v2 also identifies annotators' research background and revises documented loss weights. Conversely, v1's special four-step optimization and disabled Pearson stopping for the constant-mask benchmark are no longer specified. The explicit code-repository address is removed, although the project link and supplementary-code statement remain.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands controllable-video positioning, adding discussion of VideoComposer, CamTrol, MotionClone, DiTFlow, MOFT and other approaches. It newly identifies MinT as the closest work and distinguishes fine-grained, training-free concept timing from learned event sequencing. Motion Prompting and the spatial-awareness citation used in v1 are removed. These changes go beyond bibliography formatting.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, related-work discussion, method explanations and experimental interpretation undergo extensive rewriting. Related-work topics are reordered and broadened, energy terminology becomes magnitude, and the numbered Discussions section is replaced by separate limitations and temporal-control paragraphs. Appendix explanations and organization are also substantially revised.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn with five sampled frames instead of three and revised attention curves; Figure 3 removes the spatial-loss branch. Table 1 gains model-size information and more comparator rows while reducing metric columns. New ablation tables and semantic-failure figures are introduced, and the qualitative galleries are extensively reorganized and expanded, including a dedicated audio-comparison figure.

improvement.justification: The broader evaluated baselines, more informative component and sensitivity analyses, clearer comparison with MinT, and complete prompt inventories improve evidential support and reproducibility. These gains are tempered by removal of several video-quality metrics and the two-object ablation. An unreconciled inconsistency also remains: v2's main text says omitting timing cues leaves accuracy unchanged, while Appendix Table 7 reports 82.50% with cues versus 78.75% without. Overall, the revision provides a limited net quality improvement.
